title: Encoding categorical data
story:
A category is a name. A model needs numbers. Every way of getting from one to the other puts something into the data that the names did not contain, and the useful way to choose between them is to ask what each one asserts.

Mapping the levels to integers asserts the most and is almost always wrong. It claims an order — that the third category sits between the second and the fourth — and a spacing, that the gap between them is one unit wide and equal everywhere. For a genuinely ordered variable that may be exactly right and you should use it. For a column of cities it is a fabrication, and a model that sums across features will act on it.

Indicator columns, one per level, assert nothing at all. That honesty is the whole appeal, and the cost is width: the number of new columns is the number of distinct values, which is fine for a handful and ruinous for many. The documentation names the case plainly — high cardinality, where this encoding would inflate the feature space and make it more expensive for a downstream model to process, with location based categories such as a postal code or a region given as the classical example. There is also a linear-algebra wrinkle worth knowing: the full set of indicators sums to one in every row, so alongside an intercept term the columns are exactly collinear, which is why one level is often dropped.

The third option encodes each category by the mean of the target within it. It is compact, it is informative, and it is informative for a reason that should make you uneasy: it contains the answer. With many categories and few rows in each, a category's target mean is largely the target of the rows in it — so a feature built this way can carry a row's own outcome back into that row's features, and a model will find it.

Look at how seriously this is treated in practice. The library puts the defence inside the method rather than in a warning. Fitting and then transforming does not give the same result as fitting and transforming in one call: the combined call splits the training data into folds, by default five, and encodes each fold using the encodings learnt from the other folds. The separate fitting method learns one encoding across everything, and the documentation says it is discouraged to use it, because it can introduce data leakage. The encoded value is also shrunk toward the global mean by a smoothing factor, weighted by how many rows the category has, with the automatic setting computing that factor as an empirical Bayes estimate — a rare category is pulled most of the way back toward the overall mean, because its own mean is mostly noise.

problem.name: Categorical encoding
problem.shape: A column holds names, the model needs numbers, and the mapping between them will assert something about the names that they did not assert themselves.
tell: a column of names has been mapped to consecutive integers for convenience
the number of distinct values is in the thousands
an encoding was computed from the target
the score improved sharply when one column's encoding changed
problem.move: Pick the encoding from what it claims. Integer codes only where a real order exists. Indicator columns where the number of levels is small, dropping one level if there is an intercept. Target statistics only with cross-fitting and smoothing, computed inside the fold rather than before it — and then verify with a shuffled target that the pipeline scores at chance.
problem.invariant: Every encoding adds information that was not in the names. Order and spacing come from integer codes, width comes from indicators, and the target itself comes from target statistics — so the question is never which is best but which addition you can defend.
problem.breaks: Cross-fitting protects the training representation and not the deployment one. The encoding shipped to production is learnt from the full training set, so a category that was rare in training carries an estimate built from a handful of rows, and a category absent from training has no estimate at all — the safeguard addresses the measurement of performance, not the stability of the feature.

cost.time: cross-fitting means fitting the encoder k times rather than once, which is a constant factor on a cheap operation
cost.space: indicators cost one column per level and target encoding costs one column total, which is the entire reason the second is tempting
cost.beats: mapping names to integers, which is free and asserts an order and a spacing that the data never had

worked.problem: You encoded a high-cardinality column by its target mean and the cross-validated score jumped. What happened?
worked.reasoning:
Because the feature you built contains the target, and cross-validation was not positioned to notice.

Encoding a category by the mean of the target within it is informative in proportion to how few rows each category has. At the extreme — a category appearing once — that category's target mean is that row's target. The feature is then a copy of the answer wearing a different name, and any model will use it. High cardinality is exactly the regime where this happens, because it guarantees many sparsely populated categories.

Whether cross-validation catches it depends on where the encoding was computed. If the encoding was fitted once over the whole training set and then the folds were cut, every fold's held-out rows contributed to the means used to encode them, so the scoring rows helped build their own features. The score rises, and it rises most for the columns with the least real signal — because non-informative high-cardinality columns are the ones where the encoding is most nearly a lookup of the target.

The design response in the library is instructive. The two entry points do not agree by construction: fitting and then transforming does not equal fitting and transforming in one call. The combined call splits the training data into folds, by default five, and encodes each fold from the encodings learnt on the others, so no row contributes to its own encoding. The separate fitting method learns one encoding over everything, and the documentation explicitly discourages it for this reason.

The second defence is smoothing. The encoded value is a blend of the category's own target mean and the global mean, weighted by the category's count, so a category with two rows is pulled almost entirely back to the global mean while a category with ten thousand is left near its own. Categories unseen during fitting fall back to the global mean. That is what stops a rare level from acting as a private channel to the answer.

The diagnostic I would run is simple: compare the cross-validated score against a run where the target is shuffled. Under a shuffled target a correct pipeline scores at chance. If it still scores above chance, the encoding is leaking, and the score you were celebrating is a measurement of that leak.
worked.code:
THREE ENCODINGS, THREE ASSERTIONS

  INTEGER CODES      asserts ORDER and SPACING
     city -> 0,1,2      "2 is between 1 and 3,
                         and the gaps are equal"
     -> right for ordered data. a fabrication
        for names.

  INDICATORS         asserts NOTHING
     one column per level
     -> width == cardinality.
        fine for a handful. ruinous for many.
        docs: high cardinality "would inflate the
        feature space", e.g. zip code, region.

     wrinkle: the full set sums to 1 in every row
              -> exactly collinear with an
                 intercept -> drop one level.

  TARGET MEAN        asserts the PAST PREDICTS
     compact. informative.
     informative BECAUSE IT CONTAINS THE ANSWER.

THE LEAK, AT THE LIMIT

  a category appearing ONCE
     its target mean == that row's target
     -> the feature IS the answer, renamed.

  high cardinality guarantees many such categories.

HOW SERIOUSLY THE LIBRARY TAKES IT

  fit(X,y).transform(X)   !=   fit_transform(X,y)

     fit_transform:  splits train into k folds
                     (default 5) and encodes each
                     fold from the OTHER folds.
                     no row builds its own feature.

     fit:            one encoding over everything.
                     docs: "discouraged ... it can
                     introduce data leakage"

  the defence is IN THE METHOD, not in a warning.

SECOND DEFENCE: SMOOTHING

  encoded = blend(category mean, global mean)
            weighted by the category's COUNT

     2 rows      -> almost entirely global mean
     10,000 rows -> almost entirely its own
     unseen      -> global mean

  automatic setting: an empirical Bayes estimate.

THE DIAGNOSTIC

  shuffle the target. re-run the whole pipeline.
  a correct pipeline scores at CHANCE.
  above chance -> you are measuring the leak.

problem.practice: Take a column with many distinct values and encode it by the target mean two ways: once fitted over the whole training set before splitting, and once with cross-fitting inside the folds. Compare the scores. Then shuffle the target and run both again — one of them will still look like it is learning something.

beats.broke: A category is a name and a model needs numbers, and every route from one to the other asserts something about the categories that the names themselves never said.
beats.fix: Choose the encoding by its assertion. Integer codes claim an order and a spacing. Indicator columns claim nothing and cost one column per level. Target statistics claim that a category's history predicts its future.
beats.cost: The compact encoding is informative precisely because it contains the answer — which is why the library puts cross-fitting and smoothing inside the method and explicitly discourages the call that learns one encoding over the whole training set.

interview.q: You encoded a high-cardinality column by its target mean and the cross-validated score jumped. What happened?
interview.trap: Accepting the jump as evidence that the encoding is powerful. It is powerful in the same way an answer key is powerful, and the columns it helps most are the ones with the least real signal.
interview.answer:
Because the feature contains the target, and the cross-validation was not arranged to see it.

Encoding a category by the mean of the target within it is informative in proportion to how few rows each category holds. For a category that appears once, its target mean is that row's target — the feature is the answer under another name, and any model will find it. High cardinality is precisely the regime that produces many such sparse categories.

Whether the validation catches it depends on where the encoding was computed. If one encoding was fitted across the whole training set before the folds were cut, then every held-out row contributed to the mean used to encode it, so the scoring rows helped construct their own features. The score rises, and it rises most for the columns carrying the least genuine signal, because those are the ones where the encoding is closest to a lookup of the target.

The library's design says how seriously this is taken: fitting and then transforming deliberately does not equal fitting and transforming in one call. The combined call splits the training data into folds, five by default, and encodes each fold from the encodings learnt on the others, so no row contributes to its own encoding. The separate fitting method learns one encoding over everything and is explicitly discouraged in the documentation for this reason.

Smoothing is the second defence. The encoded value blends the category's own mean with the global mean, weighted by the category's count, so a category with two rows is pulled almost all the way back to the global mean while a large one keeps its own, and unseen categories fall back to the global mean entirely.

The check I would run is to shuffle the target and re-run the whole pipeline end to end. A correct pipeline scores at chance under a shuffled target. If it scores above chance, the encoding is leaking and the number I was pleased with is a measurement of the leak.

blueprint:
WHAT EACH ENCODING CLAIMS

   integers    order + equal spacing
   indicators  nothing  (cost: width)
   target mean the category's past predicts
               its future  (cost: it holds
               the answer)

THE WIDTH PROBLEM

   indicators:  columns == distinct values
   docs name the case: high cardinality
   "would inflate the feature space"
   classical example: zip code, region

   and: the full set sums to 1 per row
        -> collinear with an intercept
        -> drop a level

THE LEAK PROBLEM

   target mean of a category with ONE row
      == that row's target.

   high cardinality -> many such categories
   -> the feature is the answer, renamed

WHERE THE DEFENCE LIVES

   fit(X,y).transform(X) != fit_transform(X,y)

      fit_transform  -> k-fold cross fitting
                        (default 5)
                        no row encodes itself
      fit            -> "discouraged ... can
                        introduce data leakage"

   plus smoothing toward the global mean,
   weighted by the category's count.

THE TEST THAT SETTLES IT

   shuffle the target. re-run everything.
   correct pipeline -> chance.
   above chance     -> the score IS the leak.
takeaway: Every categorical encoding adds something the names did not contain — an order, a width, or the target itself — and the target one is compact and informative for the same reason it leaks, which is why cross-fitting lives inside the method rather than in a warning.
